Of course, Android does use the Linux kernel, but if you mean a systemd-and-package-manager user space, then I would ask “Why? What exactly do you imagine the advantage is?” 

There were investigations into building BSD based operating systems, and a major effort to build a from-scratch, brand-new operating system, but there were never any compelling arguments, let alone demonstrations, of why they would make anything actually better. The only real argument was that there was an existential risk that Google could cut off access to new Android developments, and my response was that even if you had to fork and maintain Android, that is still easier than starting from raw Linux.

I argued against all of the efforts, and in hindsight, I think even most of the people arguing for custom OS efforts will agree that I was right.

If you control the build, you can achieve peak performance on any given hardware component inside the framework of Android.

@ZelaLabs @davepl1968 @Dell Yes, 100% MFU would have to be at 100% utilization, but 100% MFU is impossible in practice, while 100% utilization is fairly easy.

No, you can show 100% utilization at just over idle power and pentium-level FLOPs with a single threaded kernel. The GPU isn’t completely idle, but only a tiny crumb of it is active. Power is usually a better indicator of actual utilization, but you can still optimize performance while at max power — 300W in tensor cores gets a lot more done than 300W moving memory around. NSight systems is a good step up from just GPU utilization.
@solarstrategies @davepl1968 @Dell Nsight Systems gives at least a 2D graph view of utilization, but you need Nsight Compute to get deep details about memory and tensor core utilization.

@davepl1968 @Dell GPU utilization is a measure of the time the GPU is not completely idle, it will not go down because of thermal or power throttling. If less than 100%, the GPU is going idle waiting for the CPU to give it more work.

I probably buried the lede in that one. The bit that made me curious was transformer specific. In a basic attention scheme, all of the tokens in the context attend to all the other tokens, with no sense of order whatsoever. Transformers incorporate “position encodings” with the tokens so that relative placement can be reasoned about. Systems like rope or the original transformer’s sinusoidal mappings give information about one-dimensional distance, but you could mutate the tokens on many axis to incorporate information about higher dimensional or non-uniform structure like trees or graphs.

Would it be useful? Don’t know. I’m already out of my RL lane talking about transformers, but it is an interesting thought.

I always add a few low-level player friendly rule tweaks, but my favorite house rule is “dice extension”. The old idea of a 20 being a critical hit was never sound when you might have needed a high roll even to hit. Instead, for every dice of damage or healing, if you roll the maximum value, you get to roll again and add the new value on top of the max. Repeat for additional max values. This happens often enough to add fun to normal encounters, and eventually you will have that Epic Story where all seemed lost until the die roll quadrupled up.

I did a Doom port on BeOS, and I found it very pleasant. The NeXT workstations we were using had all the 90s Unix cruft (terminfo, as you mentioned, was a good example even then), while BeOS seemed to have implemented just the core goodness.
